[37, PDF page 24] However, although the benefits of increasing whole-grain, and fruit and vegetable consumption on phytochemical and mineral micronutrient intake and public health are well documented [ 163–167], there is considerable controversy on whether, and to what extent, changing to organic food consumption can affect phytochemical and mineral micronutrient intake and associated health impacts [168,169].

paper.title: Nutritionally Improved Agricultural Crops

paper_assessments.finding: The paper reports distinctive phytochemical differences between organic and conventionally cultivated crops, but it is a TLC screening study of biomarkers and does not quantify higher concentrations of antioxidant phytochemicals in organic versus conventional crops, nor does it address the nutritional desirability of higher dietary intake. The shared entity (phytochemicals with antioxidant activity) is present in both claims, but the paper does not establish the quantitative direction of Link 1 or the nutritional-desirability association of Link 2.

edge_findings.reason: Paper reports distinctive phytochemical differences between organic and conventional crops, but does not measure higher concentrations of antioxidant phytochemicals such as phenolics; direction and metric not established.
Paper does not address dietary intake of phytochemicals or mineral micronutrients or their nutritional desirability.

connection_findings.reason: Paper shows phytochemical differences between cultivation methods but does not establish that organic crops have higher antioxidant phytochemical concentrations, so the shared-entity link to nutritional desirability is unresolved.

fragments: Furthermore, one group of TLC systems detected compounds from several of the mentioned groups. \nThe screening programme was applied in the screening of potatoes (S. tuberosum L.), peas (P. sativum L.), kale (B. oleracea L.), carrots (D. carota L.), and apples (M. domestica Borkh.), cultivated with combinations of organic and conventional methods for plant protection and nutrient supply, for phytochemical differences (biomarkers). \nDistinctive phytochemical differences were found between the differently cultivated samples of these crops.

paper.title: The Mediterranean diet and nutritional adequacy: a review.
paper.independence_group: bibliography:the mediterranean diet and nutritional adequacy a review|castro quezada i|2014

paper_assessments.finding: The paper addresses dietary antioxidants, phytochemicals and mineral micronutrients in human nutrition, but does not compare organic versus conventional crops. Edge 1 is not addressed; edge 2 is partially matched and supported as a general nutritional-desirability statement, though the paper does not explicitly discuss Zn/Se plant-food intake or organic relevance. The shared node (phytochemicals with antioxidant activity) is compatible between the two claims, but the paper provides no organic-versus-conventional composition evidence linking them.

edge_findings.reason: Paper discusses antioxidant capacity differences among foods and phytochemical classes, but never compares organic with conventional crops or reports higher phytochemical concentrations in organic crops.

Paper states higher intakes/circulating levels of antioxidant vitamins, carotenoids and flavonoids reflect lower chronic disease risk and that diets should be based on various plant foods, consistent with nutritional desirability of plant-food phytochemicals. However, it does not explicitly frame Zn/Se plant-food intake as nutritionally desirable, so match is partial.

connection_findings.reason: The shared node is phytochemicals with antioxidant activity; the paper treats these as dietary antioxidants from plant foods relevant to health, so the two claims' shared entity is biologically coherent. The paper does not, however, establish the organic-to-intake causal chain.

claim.source_local_context:
[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 2.4.1. Wheat.
[75] Studies with common wheat (T. aestivum) in the US and spelt wheat (T. spelta) in Crete reported that modern, short-straw varieties have lower mineral micronutrient (e.g., Cu, Fe, Se and/or Zn) concentrations in the grain than traditional, long-straw varieties [13,40].
[76] In a UK study with common wheat (T. aestivum), a long-straw variety from a Swiss organic breeding program was also shown to have higher levels of rust resistance, and higher phenolic concentrations than a modern, short-straw variety developed for conventional production [13].
[77] The study identified strong positive associations between foliar phenolic concentrations, and both rust and Septoria disease severity [13].
[78] In contrast, in field experiments with spelt wheat (T. spelta) in Crete, a modern shortstraw spelt variety had significantly higher grain phenolic levels than two, traditional long-straw “Urspelt” varieties and an intermediate straw-length variety developed for the organic farming sector [40].

claim.source_section_context:
[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 2.4.1. Wheat
[75, PDF page 20] Studies with common wheat (T. aestivum) in the US and spelt wheat (T. spelta) in Crete reported that modern, short-straw varieties have lower mineral micronutrient (e.g., Cu, Fe, Se and/or Zn) concentrations in the grain than traditional, long-straw varieties [13,40].
[76, PDF page 20] In a UK study with common wheat (T. aestivum), a long-straw variety from a Swiss organic breeding program was also shown to have higher levels of rust resistance, and higher phenolic concentrations than a modern, short-straw variety developed for conventional production [13].
[77, PDF page 20] The study identified strong positive associations between foliar phenolic concentrations, and both rust and Septoria disease severity [13].
[78, PDF page 20] In contrast, in field experiments with spelt wheat (T. spelta) in Crete, a modern shortstraw spelt variety had significantly higher grain phenolic levels than two, traditional long-straw “Urspelt” varieties and an intermediate straw-length variety developed for the organic farming sector [40].
[79, PDF page 20] Overall, the available evidence suggests that longer-straw wheat varieties, favored by organic farmers, have higher levels of mineral micro-nutrients, whereas there is no clear trend for a correlation between straw length and phenolic concentrations.
[80, PDF page 20] It is interesting to note that (i) the lower levels of lodging observed with manure, compared with mineral NPK fertilizer inputs, makes it less risky to use longer-straw varieties in organic farming systems, and (ii) the greater competitiveness against weeds and higher grain protein levels in longer straw varieties are a benefit in organic farming systems, which prohibit the use of water-soluble mineral N-fertilizers to increase grain protein levels, and herbicides to reduce weed competition [13,40].

project_scope.rationale: Wheat variety comparison of grain phenolic composition, a crop food-quality trait.

source_validation.rationale: Sentence states the long-straw Swiss organic variety had higher phenolic concentrations than the modern short-straw conventional variety in common wheat.

fragments: The main objective of this pilot study was therefore to compare the effect of contrasting fertilisation and crop protection regimes used in organic and conventional farming on crop health and performance parameter in two wheat varieties developed for organic/low input and conventional farming systems respectively.Results indicate that both leaf phenolic and flavonoid compounds, were positively associated with use of the ‘long straw’ variety Aszita and to a lesser extent composted FYM fertiliser inputs, while they were negatively associated with mineral N-fertiliser inputs, plant N uptake and use of the ‘short straw’ variety Solstice. On the other hand foliar and ear disease severity were positively associated with plant N uptake, use of the variety Solstice and the use of mineral fertilisers, while they were negatively associated with composted FYM fertiliser inputs, leaf phenolic/flavonoid concentrations and the use of the variety Aszita.Overall findings suggest that low input farming-focused breeding programmes might deliver varieties such as Aszita that have lower yield potential, but have higher grain protein, leaf phenolic concentrations, and foliar disease resistance under low-input conditions.

[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 4.2. Agricultural Intensification Practices have Reduced Food Quality and Safety
[57, PDF page 31] The scientific evidence now available also allows many of the differences in nutritional quality to be linked to specific agronomic practices, or the combined effect of several agronomic parameters (reviewed in part 1).
[58, PDF page 31] Most importantly, the available evidence indicates that many “innovations” (monoculture/shorter rotations, mineral N and P fertilizers, pesticides, and short-straw cereal varieties) introduced as part of the agricultural intensification (or “green revolution”) have had negative effects on both crop health and the nutritional quality and/or safety of crops.
[59, PDF page 31] Specifically, there is now substantial evidence that the use of:
[60, PDF page 31] Monoculture and short rotationsincrease crop species-specific weed, pest and disease pressure and may lead to (a) greater dependence on synthetic chemical pesticides, (b) higher pesticide residues being present in crops, and (c) a greater risk of Fusarium infection and mycotoxin contamination of cereal grains;
[61, PDF page 31] Mineral phosphorus fertilizer can (a) reduce mycorrhizal development on roots and thereby negatively affect mineral micronutrient uptake and resistance against soil-borne diseases, and (b) increase cadmium concentrations in crops;
[62, PDF page 31] Mineral nitrogen fertilizer is associated with (a) a reduction in crop resistance, (b) lower concentrations of nutritionally desirable phenolics and other resistancerelated phytochemicals/antioxidants in crops, and (c) increases the risk of Fusarium infection and mycotoxin contamination in cereal grains;
[63, PDF page 31] Synthetic chemical pesticides in agriculture are responsible for chronic dietary pesticide exposure and may reduce concentrations of certain nutritionally desirable phytochemicals/antioxidants and mineral micronutrients in crops;
[64, PDF page 31] Modern short-straw cereal varieties, (a) are less competitive against weeds and more susceptible to certain diseases (e.g., Fusarium, Septoria), (b) have lower grain protein and mineral micronutrient concentrations, and (c) increase the risk of Fusarium mycotoxin contamination in cereal grain.
[65, PDF page 31] Moreover, as described in Section 3.3.2, it is likely that current yield levels of intensive conventional crop production are not sustainable, due to the high reliance on non-renewable resources, and are likely to decline in the future when essential input becomes too expensive and/or unavailable.
[66, PDF page 31] Soil-health management based on organic matter recycling and crop fertilization methods developed by the organic farming sector may therefore become essential in maintaining future security, and allowing sustainable waste management/recycling in the future.
[67, PDF page 31] It is important to consider that there is also increasing evidence that the intensification of conventional livestock production had negative effects on the nutritional composition of both milk and meat [ 222,241–251].
[68, PDF page 31] For example, studies which compared low-input and/or organic with intensive conventional livestock production systems have shown
[69, PDF page 32] that the increased use of (i) cereal and grain/legume-based concentrate feeds, (ii) indoor production, (iii) high-yield potential dairy breeds, (iv) selection for high milk yield within breeds, and/or (iv) robotic milking systems in conventional systems may:
[70, PDF page 32] Reduce concentrations of nutritionally desirable omega-3 fatty acids in milk and meat, and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA), carotenoids and vitamin E in milk;
[71, PDF page 32] Increase levels of nutritionally undesirable saturated fatty acids (e.g., myristic and palmitic acid) in meat [222,241–251].
[72, PDF page 32] Composition differences between organic and conventional dairy products may therefore also have contributed to the differences in disease incidence between consumer cohorts with high and low organic food consumption described in Section 3.

[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 3.2. Evidence from Human Dietary Intervention and Cohort Studies.
[69] Interestingly, the same study also found that switching from habitual Western diets (with high meat and low fruit and vegetable consumption) to a healthy, traditional Mediterranean diet with low meat, and high fruit and vegetable consumption, resulted in 3–4 times higher insecticide and organophosphate exposure [ 141].
[70] These results suggest that the effects of changing to organic food consumption, considering dietary pesticide intake and the associated potential negative health impacts, may be greater with a healthy diet.
[71] The finding that organic food consumption can significantly reduce pesticide exposure is thought to be of relevance for human health, because there is increasing scientific evidence for the negative impacts of chronic dietary pesticide exposure, especially compounds that are suspected or proven to be neurotoxic and/or endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) [ 129–136].
[72] Negative health effects of occupational and environmental exposure to pesticides are also well documented and predicted to increase in the future [129,130,132–136,191].
[73] For example, a recent market analysis for pharmaceutical products that are used to treat acute carbamate and organophosphate poisoning in farmers and contractors that handle pesticides have predicted a significant increase in demand, especially in developing and underdeveloped countries, due to a predicted increase in pesticide use in these countries [191].
claim.claim_text: Chronic dietary pesticide exposure, especially to neurotoxic and endocrine-disrupting compounds, has negative impacts on human health.
claim.source_section_context:
[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 3.2. Evidence from Human Dietary Intervention and Cohort Studies
[66, PDF page 27] Several dietary intervention studies with humans and some human cohort studies have assessed the effect of organic versus conventional food consumption on urinary excretion of pesticide residues, but there is limited data on urinary excretion of other health relevant compounds (e.g., phenolics, other phytochemicals, antioxidants and mineral micronutrients).
[67, PDF page 27] These studies have consistently shown that organic food consumption results in significantly lower exposure to a range of pesticides, but identified no or only very small effects on the urinary excretion of other health relevant compounds [141,168,169,185–190]; this evidence has been described and discussed in detail in a recent systematic review by Vigar et al. [169].
[68, PDF page 27] The most controlled (during the 2-week intervention period participants consumed either only certified organic or only conventional foods) and comprehensive (in terms of the range of pesticides monitored) dietary intervention study estimated that changing to organic food consumption can reduce total pesticide exposure by more than 90% [ 141].
[69, PDF page 27] Interestingly, the same study also found that switching from habitual Western diets (with high meat and low fruit and vegetable consumption) to a healthy, traditional Mediterranean diet with low meat, and high fruit and vegetable consumption, resulted in 3–4 times higher insecticide and organophosphate exposure [ 141].
[70, PDF page 27] These results suggest that the effects of changing to organic food consumption, considering dietary pesticide intake and the associated potential negative health impacts, may be greater with a healthy diet.
[71, PDF page 27] The finding that organic food consumption can significantly reduce pesticide exposure is thought to be of relevance for human health, because there is increasing scientific evidence for the negative impacts of chronic dietary pesticide exposure, especially compounds that are suspected or proven to be neurotoxic and/or endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) [ 129–136].
[72, PDF page 27] Negative health effects of occupational and environmental exposure to pesticides are also well documented and predicted to increase in the future [129,130,132–136,191].
[73, PDF page 27] For example, a recent market analysis for pharmaceutical products that are used to treat acute carbamate and organophosphate poisoning in farmers and contractors that handle pesticides have predicted a significant increase in demand, especially in developing and underdeveloped countries, due to a predicted increase in pesticide use in these countries [191].
[74, PDF page 27] It should be pointed out that the European Commission and other government regulators set maximum residue limits (MRLs) for pesticides in food crops that are orders of magnitude below the concentrations that result in measurable toxicity symptoms in animal studies [128,161].
[75, PDF page 27] Regulators therefore consider pesticide residues below the MRLs as safe for consumers [128,129,161,192–194].
[76, PDF page 27] However, regulatory residue monitoring in Europe continues to find that a significant proportion of crop samples contain pesticide residues above the MRL [ 128], and there is increasing concern about the efficacy of the current regulatory pesticide approval system and the “safety” of pesticide residues below MRLs set by regulators [134–136].
[77, PDF page 27] One of the main concerns is that the current regulatory toxicological safety testing is based on Paracelsus’ 15th century assumption that “toxic effects” are greater at higher rather than lower doses (“the dose makes the poison”).
[78, PDF page 27] Pesticide safety testing is therefore usually based on one-generation animal studies (usually rodents) that assess the effect of high and moderate doses of chemicals.
[79, PDF page 27] Specifically, these tests determine the frequency and severity of death, disease symptoms, fetus malformations and/or low birth weights.
[80, PDF page 27] Results are then linearly extrapolated downwards and MRLs set at doses that are assumed to be safe [129,132,193–195].
[81, PDF page 27] However, many of the most widely used pesticides are suspected or confirmed endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs), which, like hormones, have (i) activity at very low doses and (ii) U-shaped and/or inverted U-shaped, non-monotonic dose-response curves [132–134,195–197].
[82, PDF page 27] This makes it impossible to predict negative health impacts associated with low-level dietary exposure based on the current regulatory, animal model-based toxicity tests.
[83, PDF page 27] Moreover, ECDs are increasingly recognized to lead to epigenetic alterations
[84, PDF page 28] and programming, which may eventually lead to an increased incidence in a variety of diseases (including obesity, type-2 diabetes, immune abnormalities and cancer) later in life, or in subsequent generations [132,195–198].
[85, PDF page 28] Epigenetic effects of ECDs can therefore only be accurately identified via extensive, multigenerational animal studies, but such tests are not usually required as part of standard regulatory pesticide safety evaluation protocols [195–198].
[86, PDF page 28] As a result, there is an urgent need to address these deficiencies, given the “health” and “societal” costs that may result from chronic exposure to EDCs both in Europe and globally [199,200].
[87, PDF page 28] There is also concern about the relatively high MRLs set by the EU for some widely used pesticides.
[88, PDF page 28] For example, MRLs for chlormequat (7 mg kg−1) and glyphosate (10 mg kg−1) are more than 10 times higher than those set for most other pesticides (0.01–0.4 mg kg−1) licensed for use in Europe [ 141,161,201,202].
[89, PDF page 28] In this context, it is important to consider that both pesticides are suspected endocrine-disrupting chemicals [203] and glyphosate was recently classified as a probable carcinogen [204].
[90, PDF page 28] Another limitation of the current regulatory toxicological evaluations is that they only require testing of individual active compounds, whereas testing of formulated products and combinations of pesticides is not usually required [129,132,193–195].
[91, PDF page 28] Moreover, the reliance of regulators on industry-commissioned (rather than independent) toxicological evaluations has recently been criticized [205,206].
[92, PDF page 28] A recent systematic review reported that there have been no controlled dietary intervention studies/clinical trials in which the effects of organic versus conventional food production on health outcomes has been studied [169].
[93, PDF page 28] However, there is increasing evidence from human cohort/epidemiological studies that organic food consumption is associated with significantly lower risks of a range of diseases including overweight/obesity [207], metabolic syndrome [208], certain cancers [209,210], hypospadias [211,212] pre-eclampsia [213], eczema [214] and middle ear infections (otitis media) [215].
[94, PDF page 28] This evidence has been discussed in detail in a recent systematic review by Vigar et al. [169].
[95, PDF page 28] Associations between disease incidence and pesticide exposure were only assessed in one of these observational studies, which found that the presence of metabolites of triazine herbicides in urine was positively associated with recurrent middle ear infections in infants [169,215].
[96, PDF page 28] It is important to note that there are now two European studies from France and the UK, which have reported that organic food consumption results in a lower incidence of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) [ 209,210] and that observational evidence for positive associations between NHL and exposure to organophosphates were the main reasons why glyphosate and other organophosphates are now as classified as probable carcinogens [204].
[97, PDF page 28] Lower pesticide exposure from fruit and vegetable consumption was recently found to be associated with improved reproductive health parameters in both men and women[216,217].
[98, PDF page 28] Similarly , a reduced incidence of breast cancer among postmenopausal women in the NutriNet- Santé cohort was linked to (i) low dietary exposure to synthetic pesticides such as chlorpyriphos, imazalil, malathion and thiabendazole [218], and (ii) high organic food consumption [210].

paper_assessments.finding: The paper documents widespread synthetic pesticide use and food contamination in the EU and supports neurotoxic/developmental health concerns, but it does not establish that agricultural pesticide use causes chronic dietary exposure as a causal claim, nor does it cover endocrine-disrupting compounds or general negative health impacts beyond neurodevelopment.

edge_findings.reason: Paper shows synthetic pesticides applied to food crops and residues commonly contaminating foods, consistent with a dietary exposure pathway, but frames it as contamination/residue occurrence rather than explicitly asserting causation of chronic dietary exposure.

Paper supports negative neurodevelopmental health impacts of neurotoxic pesticide exposure, but addresses developmental neurotoxicity, not the full claim including endocrine-disrupting compounds and broad human health impacts.

claim.source_section_context:
[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 4.2. Agricultural Intensification Practices have Reduced Food Quality and Safety
[57, PDF page 31] The scientific evidence now available also allows many of the differences in nutritional quality to be linked to specific agronomic practices, or the combined effect of several agronomic parameters (reviewed in part 1).
[58, PDF page 31] Most importantly, the available evidence indicates that many “innovations” (monoculture/shorter rotations, mineral N and P fertilizers, pesticides, and short-straw cereal varieties) introduced as part of the agricultural intensification (or “green revolution”) have had negative effects on both crop health and the nutritional quality and/or safety of crops.
[59, PDF page 31] Specifically, there is now substantial evidence that the use of:
[60, PDF page 31] Monoculture and short rotationsincrease crop species-specific weed, pest and disease pressure and may lead to (a) greater dependence on synthetic chemical pesticides, (b) higher pesticide residues being present in crops, and (c) a greater risk of Fusarium infection and mycotoxin contamination of cereal grains;
[61, PDF page 31] Mineral phosphorus fertilizer can (a) reduce mycorrhizal development on roots and thereby negatively affect mineral micronutrient uptake and resistance against soil-borne diseases, and (b) increase cadmium concentrations in crops;
[62, PDF page 31] Mineral nitrogen fertilizer is associated with (a) a reduction in crop resistance, (b) lower concentrations of nutritionally desirable phenolics and other resistancerelated phytochemicals/antioxidants in crops, and (c) increases the risk of Fusarium infection and mycotoxin contamination in cereal grains;
[63, PDF page 31] Synthetic chemical pesticides in agriculture are responsible for chronic dietary pesticide exposure and may reduce concentrations of certain nutritionally desirable phytochemicals/antioxidants and mineral micronutrients in crops;
[64, PDF page 31] Modern short-straw cereal varieties, (a) are less competitive against weeds and more susceptible to certain diseases (e.g., Fusarium, Septoria), (b) have lower grain protein and mineral micronutrient concentrations, and (c) increase the risk of Fusarium mycotoxin contamination in cereal grain.
[65, PDF page 31] Moreover, as described in Section 3.3.2, it is likely that current yield levels of intensive conventional crop production are not sustainable, due to the high reliance on non-renewable resources, and are likely to decline in the future when essential input becomes too expensive and/or unavailable.
[66, PDF page 31] Soil-health management based on organic matter recycling and crop fertilization methods developed by the organic farming sector may therefore become essential in maintaining future security, and allowing sustainable waste management/recycling in the future.
[67, PDF page 31] It is important to consider that there is also increasing evidence that the intensification of conventional livestock production had negative effects on the nutritional composition of both milk and meat [ 222,241–251].
[68, PDF page 31] For example, studies which compared low-input and/or organic with intensive conventional livestock production systems have shown
[69, PDF page 32] that the increased use of (i) cereal and grain/legume-based concentrate feeds, (ii) indoor production, (iii) high-yield potential dairy breeds, (iv) selection for high milk yield within breeds, and/or (iv) robotic milking systems in conventional systems may:
[70, PDF page 32] Reduce concentrations of nutritionally desirable omega-3 fatty acids in milk and meat, and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA), carotenoids and vitamin E in milk;
[71, PDF page 32] Increase levels of nutritionally undesirable saturated fatty acids (e.g., myristic and palmitic acid) in meat [222,241–251].
[72, PDF page 32] Composition differences between organic and conventional dairy products may therefore also have contributed to the differences in disease incidence between consumer cohorts with high and low organic food consumption described in Section 3.

claim.source_section_context:
[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 3.2. Evidence from Human Dietary Intervention and Cohort Studies
[66, PDF page 27] Several dietary intervention studies with humans and some human cohort studies have assessed the effect of organic versus conventional food consumption on urinary excretion of pesticide residues, but there is limited data on urinary excretion of other health relevant compounds (e.g., phenolics, other phytochemicals, antioxidants and mineral micronutrients).
[67, PDF page 27] These studies have consistently shown that organic food consumption results in significantly lower exposure to a range of pesticides, but identified no or only very small effects on the urinary excretion of other health relevant compounds [141,168,169,185–190]; this evidence has been described and discussed in detail in a recent systematic review by Vigar et al. [169].
[68, PDF page 27] The most controlled (during the 2-week intervention period participants consumed either only certified organic or only conventional foods) and comprehensive (in terms of the range of pesticides monitored) dietary intervention study estimated that changing to organic food consumption can reduce total pesticide exposure by more than 90% [ 141].
[69, PDF page 27] Interestingly, the same study also found that switching from habitual Western diets (with high meat and low fruit and vegetable consumption) to a healthy, traditional Mediterranean diet with low meat, and high fruit and vegetable consumption, resulted in 3–4 times higher insecticide and organophosphate exposure [ 141].
[70, PDF page 27] These results suggest that the effects of changing to organic food consumption, considering dietary pesticide intake and the associated potential negative health impacts, may be greater with a healthy diet.
[71, PDF page 27] The finding that organic food consumption can significantly reduce pesticide exposure is thought to be of relevance for human health, because there is increasing scientific evidence for the negative impacts of chronic dietary pesticide exposure, especially compounds that are suspected or proven to be neurotoxic and/or endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) [ 129–136].
[72, PDF page 27] Negative health effects of occupational and environmental exposure to pesticides are also well documented and predicted to increase in the future [129,130,132–136,191].
[73, PDF page 27] For example, a recent market analysis for pharmaceutical products that are used to treat acute carbamate and organophosphate poisoning in farmers and contractors that handle pesticides have predicted a significant increase in demand, especially in developing and underdeveloped countries, due to a predicted increase in pesticide use in these countries [191].
[74, PDF page 27] It should be pointed out that the European Commission and other government regulators set maximum residue limits (MRLs) for pesticides in food crops that are orders of magnitude below the concentrations that result in measurable toxicity symptoms in animal studies [128,161].
[75, PDF page 27] Regulators therefore consider pesticide residues below the MRLs as safe for consumers [128,129,161,192–194].
[76, PDF page 27] However, regulatory residue monitoring in Europe continues to find that a significant proportion of crop samples contain pesticide residues above the MRL [ 128], and there is increasing concern about the efficacy of the current regulatory pesticide approval system and the “safety” of pesticide residues below MRLs set by regulators [134–136].
[77, PDF page 27] One of the main concerns is that the current regulatory toxicological safety testing is based on Paracelsus’ 15th century assumption that “toxic effects” are greater at higher rather than lower doses (“the dose makes the poison”).
[78, PDF page 27] Pesticide safety testing is therefore usually based on one-generation animal studies (usually rodents) that assess the effect of high and moderate doses of chemicals.
[79, PDF page 27] Specifically, these tests determine the frequency and severity of death, disease symptoms, fetus malformations and/or low birth weights.
[80, PDF page 27] Results are then linearly extrapolated downwards and MRLs set at doses that are assumed to be safe [129,132,193–195].
[81, PDF page 27] However, many of the most widely used pesticides are suspected or confirmed endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs), which, like hormones, have (i) activity at very low doses and (ii) U-shaped and/or inverted U-shaped, non-monotonic dose-response curves [132–134,195–197].
[82, PDF page 27] This makes it impossible to predict negative health impacts associated with low-level dietary exposure based on the current regulatory, animal model-based toxicity tests.
[83, PDF page 27] Moreover, ECDs are increasingly recognized to lead to epigenetic alterations
[84, PDF page 28] and programming, which may eventually lead to an increased incidence in a variety of diseases (including obesity, type-2 diabetes, immune abnormalities and cancer) later in life, or in subsequent generations [132,195–198].
[85, PDF page 28] Epigenetic effects of ECDs can therefore only be accurately identified via extensive, multigenerational animal studies, but such tests are not usually required as part of standard regulatory pesticide safety evaluation protocols [195–198].
[86, PDF page 28] As a result, there is an urgent need to address these deficiencies, given the “health” and “societal” costs that may result from chronic exposure to EDCs both in Europe and globally [199,200].
[87, PDF page 28] There is also concern about the relatively high MRLs set by the EU for some widely used pesticides.
[88, PDF page 28] For example, MRLs for chlormequat (7 mg kg−1) and glyphosate (10 mg kg−1) are more than 10 times higher than those set for most other pesticides (0.01–0.4 mg kg−1) licensed for use in Europe [ 141,161,201,202].
[89, PDF page 28] In this context, it is important to consider that both pesticides are suspected endocrine-disrupting chemicals [203] and glyphosate was recently classified as a probable carcinogen [204].
[90, PDF page 28] Another limitation of the current regulatory toxicological evaluations is that they only require testing of individual active compounds, whereas testing of formulated products and combinations of pesticides is not usually required [129,132,193–195].
[91, PDF page 28] Moreover, the reliance of regulators on industry-commissioned (rather than independent) toxicological evaluations has recently been criticized [205,206].
[92, PDF page 28] A recent systematic review reported that there have been no controlled dietary intervention studies/clinical trials in which the effects of organic versus conventional food production on health outcomes has been studied [169].
[93, PDF page 28] However, there is increasing evidence from human cohort/epidemiological studies that organic food consumption is associated with significantly lower risks of a range of diseases including overweight/obesity [207], metabolic syndrome [208], certain cancers [209,210], hypospadias [211,212] pre-eclampsia [213], eczema [214] and middle ear infections (otitis media) [215].
[94, PDF page 28] This evidence has been discussed in detail in a recent systematic review by Vigar et al. [169].
[95, PDF page 28] Associations between disease incidence and pesticide exposure were only assessed in one of these observational studies, which found that the presence of metabolites of triazine herbicides in urine was positively associated with recurrent middle ear infections in infants [169,215].
[96, PDF page 28] It is important to note that there are now two European studies from France and the UK, which have reported that organic food consumption results in a lower incidence of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) [ 209,210] and that observational evidence for positive associations between NHL and exposure to organophosphates were the main reasons why glyphosate and other organophosphates are now as classified as probable carcinogens [204].
[97, PDF page 28] Lower pesticide exposure from fruit and vegetable consumption was recently found to be associated with improved reproductive health parameters in both men and women[216,217].
[98, PDF page 28] Similarly , a reduced incidence of breast cancer among postmenopausal women in the NutriNet- Santé cohort was linked to (i) low dietary exposure to synthetic pesticides such as chlorpyriphos, imazalil, malathion and thiabendazole [218], and (ii) high organic food consumption [210].

fragments: Results: Compared with men in the highest tertile of fruit and vegetable consumption (≥5.17 servings/day), those in the lowest tertile (≤3.23 servings/day) showed a higher prevalence of abnormal sperm concentration (49% vs. 21%), abnormal total sperm count (53% vs. 22%), and reduced total and progressive sperm motility (74% vs. 46% and 73% vs. 53%, respectively) (all P<0.05).

Similarly, women in the highest tertile of fruit and vegetable consumption (≥4.87 servings/day) achieved higher rates of clinical pregnancy and live birth (52% vs. 29% and 52% vs. 25%, respectively) compared with women in the lowest tertile (≤2.86 servings/day).

claim.source_section_context:
[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 4.2. Agricultural Intensification Practices have Reduced Food Quality and Safety
[57, PDF page 31] The scientific evidence now available also allows many of the differences in nutritional quality to be linked to specific agronomic practices, or the combined effect of several agronomic parameters (reviewed in part 1).
[58, PDF page 31] Most importantly, the available evidence indicates that many “innovations” (monoculture/shorter rotations, mineral N and P fertilizers, pesticides, and short-straw cereal varieties) introduced as part of the agricultural intensification (or “green revolution”) have had negative effects on both crop health and the nutritional quality and/or safety of crops.
[59, PDF page 31] Specifically, there is now substantial evidence that the use of:
[60, PDF page 31] Monoculture and short rotationsincrease crop species-specific weed, pest and disease pressure and may lead to (a) greater dependence on synthetic chemical pesticides, (b) higher pesticide residues being present in crops, and (c) a greater risk of Fusarium infection and mycotoxin contamination of cereal grains;
[61, PDF page 31] Mineral phosphorus fertilizer can (a) reduce mycorrhizal development on roots and thereby negatively affect mineral micronutrient uptake and resistance against soil-borne diseases, and (b) increase cadmium concentrations in crops;
[62, PDF page 31] Mineral nitrogen fertilizer is associated with (a) a reduction in crop resistance, (b) lower concentrations of nutritionally desirable phenolics and other resistancerelated phytochemicals/antioxidants in crops, and (c) increases the risk of Fusarium infection and mycotoxin contamination in cereal grains;
[63, PDF page 31] Synthetic chemical pesticides in agriculture are responsible for chronic dietary pesticide exposure and may reduce concentrations of certain nutritionally desirable phytochemicals/antioxidants and mineral micronutrients in crops;
[64, PDF page 31] Modern short-straw cereal varieties, (a) are less competitive against weeds and more susceptible to certain diseases (e.g., Fusarium, Septoria), (b) have lower grain protein and mineral micronutrient concentrations, and (c) increase the risk of Fusarium mycotoxin contamination in cereal grain.
[65, PDF page 31] Moreover, as described in Section 3.3.2, it is likely that current yield levels of intensive conventional crop production are not sustainable, due to the high reliance on non-renewable resources, and are likely to decline in the future when essential input becomes too expensive and/or unavailable.
[66, PDF page 31] Soil-health management based on organic matter recycling and crop fertilization methods developed by the organic farming sector may therefore become essential in maintaining future security, and allowing sustainable waste management/recycling in the future.
[67, PDF page 31] It is important to consider that there is also increasing evidence that the intensification of conventional livestock production had negative effects on the nutritional composition of both milk and meat [ 222,241–251].
[68, PDF page 31] For example, studies which compared low-input and/or organic with intensive conventional livestock production systems have shown
[69, PDF page 32] that the increased use of (i) cereal and grain/legume-based concentrate feeds, (ii) indoor production, (iii) high-yield potential dairy breeds, (iv) selection for high milk yield within breeds, and/or (iv) robotic milking systems in conventional systems may:
[70, PDF page 32] Reduce concentrations of nutritionally desirable omega-3 fatty acids in milk and meat, and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA), carotenoids and vitamin E in milk;
[71, PDF page 32] Increase levels of nutritionally undesirable saturated fatty acids (e.g., myristic and palmitic acid) in meat [222,241–251].
[72, PDF page 32] Composition differences between organic and conventional dairy products may therefore also have contributed to the differences in disease incidence between consumer cohorts with high and low organic food consumption described in Section 3.

claim.source_local_context:
[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 3.2. Evidence from Human Dietary Intervention and Cohort Studies.
[14] Lower pesticide exposure from fruit and vegetable consumption was recently found to be associated with improved reproductive health parameters in both men and women[216,217].
[15] Similarly , a reduced incidence of breast cancer among postmenopausal women in the NutriNet- Santé cohort was linked to (i) low dietary exposure to synthetic pesticides such as chlorpyriphos, imazalil, malathion and thiabendazole [218], and (ii) high organic food consumption [210].
[16] However, although both animal dietary intervention studies and observational research suggest that lower pesticide exposure may at least partially explain the health benefits associated with organic food consumption, there is still considerable uncertainty, whether and to what extent dietary pesticide exposure is responsible for the positive health impacts linked to organic food intake [169].
[17] This uncertainty is mainly due to the lack of corroborating evidence from clinical trials, but also the finding that organic and conventional food consumers differ in other lifestyle parameters, which may have confounded results [169].
[18] For example, organic consumers were reported to do more exercise and have healthier diets [219–221].

[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 3.2. Evidence from Human Dietary Intervention and Cohort Studies
[1, PDF page 28] and programming, which may eventually lead to an increased incidence in a variety of diseases (including obesity, type-2 diabetes, immune abnormalities and cancer) later in life, or in subsequent generations [132,195–198].
[2, PDF page 28] Epigenetic effects of ECDs can therefore only be accurately identified via extensive, multigenerational animal studies, but such tests are not usually required as part of standard regulatory pesticide safety evaluation protocols [195–198].
[3, PDF page 28] As a result, there is an urgent need to address these deficiencies, given the “health” and “societal” costs that may result from chronic exposure to EDCs both in Europe and globally [199,200].
[4, PDF page 28] There is also concern about the relatively high MRLs set by the EU for some widely used pesticides.
[5, PDF page 28] For example, MRLs for chlormequat (7 mg kg−1) and glyphosate (10 mg kg−1) are more than 10 times higher than those set for most other pesticides (0.01–0.4 mg kg−1) licensed for use in Europe [ 141,161,201,202].
[6, PDF page 28] In this context, it is important to consider that both pesticides are suspected endocrine-disrupting chemicals [203] and glyphosate was recently classified as a probable carcinogen [204].
[7, PDF page 28] Another limitation of the current regulatory toxicological evaluations is that they only require testing of individual active compounds, whereas testing of formulated products and combinations of pesticides is not usually required [129,132,193–195].
[8, PDF page 28] Moreover, the reliance of regulators on industry-commissioned (rather than independent) toxicological evaluations has recently been criticized [205,206].
[9, PDF page 28] A recent systematic review reported that there have been no controlled dietary intervention studies/clinical trials in which the effects of organic versus conventional food production on health outcomes has been studied [169].
[10, PDF page 28] However, there is increasing evidence from human cohort/epidemiological studies that organic food consumption is associated with significantly lower risks of a range of diseases including overweight/obesity [207], metabolic syndrome [208], certain cancers [209,210], hypospadias [211,212] pre-eclampsia [213], eczema [214] and middle ear infections (otitis media) [215].
[11, PDF page 28] This evidence has been discussed in detail in a recent systematic review by Vigar et al. [169].
[12, PDF page 28] Associations between disease incidence and pesticide exposure were only assessed in one of these observational studies, which found that the presence of metabolites of triazine herbicides in urine was positively associated with recurrent middle ear infections in infants [169,215].
[13, PDF page 28] It is important to note that there are now two European studies from France and the UK, which have reported that organic food consumption results in a lower incidence of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) [ 209,210] and that observational evidence for positive associations between NHL and exposure to organophosphates were the main reasons why glyphosate and other organophosphates are now as classified as probable carcinogens [204].
[14, PDF page 28] Lower pesticide exposure from fruit and vegetable consumption was recently found to be associated with improved reproductive health parameters in both men and women[216,217].
[15, PDF page 28] Similarly , a reduced incidence of breast cancer among postmenopausal women in the NutriNet- Santé cohort was linked to (i) low dietary exposure to synthetic pesticides such as chlorpyriphos, imazalil, malathion and thiabendazole [218], and (ii) high organic food consumption [210].
[16, PDF page 28] However, although both animal dietary intervention studies and observational research suggest that lower pesticide exposure may at least partially explain the health benefits associated with organic food consumption, there is still considerable uncertainty, whether and to what extent dietary pesticide exposure is responsible for the positive health impacts linked to organic food intake [169].

[18] Moreover, we summarize our current understanding of how quality gains are linked to the implementation of the “innovations” introduced into conventional crop production during the intensification or “green revolution” of agriculture over the last 100 years.
[19] In the second part of the article, we critically review the evidence for the range of health benefits related to organic food consumption.
[20] Specifically, we describe and discuss the results from: (i) dietary intervention studies which have found that organic food consumption substantially reduces pesticide exposure in humans and affects feed intake, growth, hormone balances and immune system responsiveness in animal models; (ii) human cohort/epidemiological studies which have reported significant positive associations between organic food consumption and the lower incidence of a range of diseases including obesity, metabolic syndrome, cancer, hypospadias, pre-eclampsia, eczema and middle ear infections in infants; (iii) interactions and trade-offs between diet (e.g., whole-grain, fruit and vegetables and reduced red-meat consumption) and food types (organic versus conventional) concerning public health and future food security.
[21] The article also identifies knowledge gaps and highlights the need for (i) longterm, factorial field experiments to understand the relative effects of agronomic and pedoclimatic drivers on crop quality and safety, and (ii) clinical trials and additional human cohort studies to confirm the positive health outcomes linked to organic food consumption.
[22] The main conclusions from our review are that there is growing evidence that (i) agricultural intensification has resulted in a reduction in the nutritional quality of food and the sustainability of food production, and (ii) organic farming practices not only improve food quality and human health, but also food security.

[16, PDF page 2] The environmental and biodiversity benefits of organic farming are widely recognized, but there is still controversy about the effects of organic production methods on the nutritional composition of food and human health.
[17, PDF page 2] In the first part of this article therefore, we critically review the evidence that organic farming methods improve the nutritional quality of food crops.
[18, PDF page 2] Moreover, we summarize our current understanding of how quality gains are linked to the implementation of the “innovations” introduced into conventional crop production during the intensification or “green revolution” of agriculture over the last 100 years.
[19, PDF page 2] In the second part of the article, we critically review the evidence for the range of health benefits related to organic food consumption.
[20, PDF page 2] Specifically, we describe and discuss the results from: (i) dietary intervention studies which have found that organic food consumption substantially reduces pesticide exposure in humans and affects feed intake, growth, hormone balances and immune system responsiveness in animal models; (ii) human cohort/epidemiological studies which have reported significant positive associations between organic food consumption and the lower incidence of a range of diseases including obesity, metabolic syndrome, cancer, hypospadias, pre-eclampsia, eczema and middle ear infections in infants; (iii) interactions and trade-offs between diet (e.g., whole-grain, fruit and vegetables and reduced red-meat consumption) and food types (organic versus conventional) concerning public health and future food security.
[21, PDF page 2] The article also identifies knowledge gaps and highlights the need for (i) longterm, factorial field experiments to understand the relative effects of agronomic and pedoclimatic drivers on crop quality and safety, and (ii) clinical trials and additional human cohort studies to confirm the positive health outcomes linked to organic food consumption.
[22, PDF page 2] The main conclusions from our review are that there is growing evidence that (i) agricultural intensification has resulted in a reduction in the nutritional quality of food and the sustainability of food production, and (ii) organic farming practices not only improve food quality and human health, but also food security.
[23, PDF page 2] This is particularly true where current nutritional guidelines (increasing whole-grain, fruit and vegetable products, while reducing red-meat consumption) are implemented.

[69] Interestingly, the same study also found that switching from habitual Western diets (with high meat and low fruit and vegetable consumption) to a healthy, traditional Mediterranean diet with low meat, and high fruit and vegetable consumption, resulted in 3–4 times higher insecticide and organophosphate exposure [ 141].
[70] These results suggest that the effects of changing to organic food consumption, considering dietary pesticide intake and the associated potential negative health impacts, may be greater with a healthy diet.
[71] The finding that organic food consumption can significantly reduce pesticide exposure is thought to be of relevance for human health, because there is increasing scientific evidence for the negative impacts of chronic dietary pesticide exposure, especially compounds that are suspected or proven to be neurotoxic and/or endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) [ 129–136].
[72] Negative health effects of occupational and environmental exposure to pesticides are also well documented and predicted to increase in the future [129,130,132–136,191].
[73] For example, a recent market analysis for pharmaceutical products that are used to treat acute carbamate and organophosphate poisoning in farmers and contractors that handle pesticides have predicted a significant increase in demand, especially in developing and underdeveloped countries, due to a predicted increase in pesticide use in these countries [191].

claim.source_section_context:
[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 3.2. Evidence from Human Dietary Intervention and Cohort Studies
[66, PDF page 27] Several dietary intervention studies with humans and some human cohort studies have assessed the effect of organic versus conventional food consumption on urinary excretion of pesticide residues, but there is limited data on urinary excretion of other health relevant compounds (e.g., phenolics, other phytochemicals, antioxidants and mineral micronutrients).
[67, PDF page 27] These studies have consistently shown that organic food consumption results in significantly lower exposure to a range of pesticides, but identified no or only very small effects on the urinary excretion of other health relevant compounds [141,168,169,185–190]; this evidence has been described and discussed in detail in a recent systematic review by Vigar et al. [169].
[68, PDF page 27] The most controlled (during the 2-week intervention period participants consumed either only certified organic or only conventional foods) and comprehensive (in terms of the range of pesticides monitored) dietary intervention study estimated that changing to organic food consumption can reduce total pesticide exposure by more than 90% [ 141].
[69, PDF page 27] Interestingly, the same study also found that switching from habitual Western diets (with high meat and low fruit and vegetable consumption) to a healthy, traditional Mediterranean diet with low meat, and high fruit and vegetable consumption, resulted in 3–4 times higher insecticide and organophosphate exposure [ 141].
[70, PDF page 27] These results suggest that the effects of changing to organic food consumption, considering dietary pesticide intake and the associated potential negative health impacts, may be greater with a healthy diet.
[71, PDF page 27] The finding that organic food consumption can significantly reduce pesticide exposure is thought to be of relevance for human health, because there is increasing scientific evidence for the negative impacts of chronic dietary pesticide exposure, especially compounds that are suspected or proven to be neurotoxic and/or endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) [ 129–136].
[72, PDF page 27] Negative health effects of occupational and environmental exposure to pesticides are also well documented and predicted to increase in the future [129,130,132–136,191].
[73, PDF page 27] For example, a recent market analysis for pharmaceutical products that are used to treat acute carbamate and organophosphate poisoning in farmers and contractors that handle pesticides have predicted a significant increase in demand, especially in developing and underdeveloped countries, due to a predicted increase in pesticide use in these countries [191].
[74, PDF page 27] It should be pointed out that the European Commission and other government regulators set maximum residue limits (MRLs) for pesticides in food crops that are orders of magnitude below the concentrations that result in measurable toxicity symptoms in animal studies [128,161].
[75, PDF page 27] Regulators therefore consider pesticide residues below the MRLs as safe for consumers [128,129,161,192–194].
[76, PDF page 27] However, regulatory residue monitoring in Europe continues to find that a significant proportion of crop samples contain pesticide residues above the MRL [ 128], and there is increasing concern about the efficacy of the current regulatory pesticide approval system and the “safety” of pesticide residues below MRLs set by regulators [134–136].
[77, PDF page 27] One of the main concerns is that the current regulatory toxicological safety testing is based on Paracelsus’ 15th century assumption that “toxic effects” are greater at higher rather than lower doses (“the dose makes the poison”).
[78, PDF page 27] Pesticide safety testing is therefore usually based on one-generation animal studies (usually rodents) that assess the effect of high and moderate doses of chemicals.
[79, PDF page 27] Specifically, these tests determine the frequency and severity of death, disease symptoms, fetus malformations and/or low birth weights.
[80, PDF page 27] Results are then linearly extrapolated downwards and MRLs set at doses that are assumed to be safe [129,132,193–195].
[81, PDF page 27] However, many of the most widely used pesticides are suspected or confirmed endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs), which, like hormones, have (i) activity at very low doses and (ii) U-shaped and/or inverted U-shaped, non-monotonic dose-response curves [132–134,195–197].
[82, PDF page 27] This makes it impossible to predict negative health impacts associated with low-level dietary exposure based on the current regulatory, animal model-based toxicity tests.
[83, PDF page 27] Moreover, ECDs are increasingly recognized to lead to epigenetic alterations
[84, PDF page 28] and programming, which may eventually lead to an increased incidence in a variety of diseases (including obesity, type-2 diabetes, immune abnormalities and cancer) later in life, or in subsequent generations [132,195–198].
[85, PDF page 28] Epigenetic effects of ECDs can therefore only be accurately identified via extensive, multigenerational animal studies, but such tests are not usually required as part of standard regulatory pesticide safety evaluation protocols [195–198].
[86, PDF page 28] As a result, there is an urgent need to address these deficiencies, given the “health” and “societal” costs that may result from chronic exposure to EDCs both in Europe and globally [199,200].
[87, PDF page 28] There is also concern about the relatively high MRLs set by the EU for some widely used pesticides.
[88, PDF page 28] For example, MRLs for chlormequat (7 mg kg−1) and glyphosate (10 mg kg−1) are more than 10 times higher than those set for most other pesticides (0.01–0.4 mg kg−1) licensed for use in Europe [ 141,161,201,202].
[89, PDF page 28] In this context, it is important to consider that both pesticides are suspected endocrine-disrupting chemicals [203] and glyphosate was recently classified as a probable carcinogen [204].
[90, PDF page 28] Another limitation of the current regulatory toxicological evaluations is that they only require testing of individual active compounds, whereas testing of formulated products and combinations of pesticides is not usually required [129,132,193–195].
[91, PDF page 28] Moreover, the reliance of regulators on industry-commissioned (rather than independent) toxicological evaluations has recently been criticized [205,206].
[92, PDF page 28] A recent systematic review reported that there have been no controlled dietary intervention studies/clinical trials in which the effects of organic versus conventional food production on health outcomes has been studied [169].
[93, PDF page 28] However, there is increasing evidence from human cohort/epidemiological studies that organic food consumption is associated with significantly lower risks of a range of diseases including overweight/obesity [207], metabolic syndrome [208], certain cancers [209,210], hypospadias [211,212] pre-eclampsia [213], eczema [214] and middle ear infections (otitis media) [215].
[94, PDF page 28] This evidence has been discussed in detail in a recent systematic review by Vigar et al. [169].
[95, PDF page 28] Associations between disease incidence and pesticide exposure were only assessed in one of these observational studies, which found that the presence of metabolites of triazine herbicides in urine was positively associated with recurrent middle ear infections in infants [169,215].
[96, PDF page 28] It is important to note that there are now two European studies from France and the UK, which have reported that organic food consumption results in a lower incidence of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) [ 209,210] and that observational evidence for positive associations between NHL and exposure to organophosphates were the main reasons why glyphosate and other organophosphates are now as classified as probable carcinogens [204].
[97, PDF page 28] Lower pesticide exposure from fruit and vegetable consumption was recently found to be associated with improved reproductive health parameters in both men and women[216,217].
[98, PDF page 28] Similarly , a reduced incidence of breast cancer among postmenopausal women in the NutriNet- Santé cohort was linked to (i) low dietary exposure to synthetic pesticides such as chlorpyriphos, imazalil, malathion and thiabendazole [218], and (ii) high organic food consumption [210].

fragments: On 26 and 27 November 2009, 29 experts met in Brussels to discuss current opinions on the effects of dietary exposure to endocrine-active pesticide residues.Representatives from academia, industry, government and non-profit organisations participated in a workshop combining expert lectures and breakout sessions.The workshop was organised such that 8 presentations by experts with specialties in different aspects of endocrine disruption were followed by a breakout group session.Each of the 4 breakout groups discussed 2 questions posed to them by the workshop organisers and then gave a short presentation on their responses to the questions, including whether or not they reached consensus on those responses.In the pages that follow, the 8 expert presentations and the presentations from the breakout sessions are summarised in detail.Interestingly, only one of the breakout groups was able to say that they had no significant disagreements, and for 3 of the questions 2 groups indicated that they could not reach any significant agreement at all ('Is endocrine disruption a mechanism essentially different from other toxicological mechanisms?', 'Should [endocrine disrupting chemicals] therefore be regulated using different criteria?' and 'Is the effort currently dedicated to this subject [of pesticides with potentially endocrine disrupting properties] proportional to the real health risk?').In each of these cases, the reason for the lack of consensus was attributed to a lack of adequate knowledge: Either on how to measure endocrine effects or on what the real health risks of Environment International 37 (2011) 980-990

edges.paper: Integrated Soil and Crop Management in Organic Agriculture: A Logical Framework to Ensure Food Quality and Human Health?
edges.subject: Organic food
edges.claim_text: Organic food consumption substantially reduces pesticide exposure in humans, according to dietary intervention studies.
edges.quote: Specifically, we describe and discuss the results from: (i) dietary intervention studies which have found that organic food consumption substantially reduces pesticide exposure in humans and affects feed intake, growth, hormone balances and immune system responsiveness in animal models; (ii) human cohort/epidemiological studies which have reported significant positive associations between organic food consumption and the lower incidence of a range of diseases including obesity, metabolic syndrome, cancer, hypospadias, pre-eclampsia, eczema and middle ear infections in infants; (iii) interactions and trade-offs between diet (e.g., whole-grain, fruit and vegetables and reduced red-meat consumption) and food types (organic versus conventional) concerning public health and future food security.

project_scope.rationale: Organic food consumption reducing human pesticide exposure is a food-safety/human-exposure pathway segment.

edges.quote: Lower pesticide exposure from fruit and vegetable consumption was recently found to be associated with improved reproductive health parameters in both men and women[216,217].

[20] Specifically, we describe and discuss the results from: (i) dietary intervention studies which have found that organic food consumption substantially reduces pesticide exposure in humans and affects feed intake, growth, hormone balances and immune system responsiveness in animal models; (ii) human cohort/epidemiological studies which have reported significant positive associations between organic food consumption and the lower incidence of a range of diseases including obesity, metabolic syndrome, cancer, hypospadias, pre-eclampsia, eczema and middle ear infections in infants; (iii) interactions and trade-offs between diet (e.g., whole-grain, fruit and vegetables and reduced red-meat consumption) and food types (organic versus conventional) concerning public health and future food security.
[21] The article also identifies knowledge gaps and highlights the need for (i) longterm, factorial field experiments to understand the relative effects of agronomic and pedoclimatic drivers on crop quality and safety, and (ii) clinical trials and additional human cohort studies to confirm the positive health outcomes linked to organic food consumption.

[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] Abstract
[16, PDF page 2] The environmental and biodiversity benefits of organic farming are widely recognized, but there is still controversy about the effects of organic production methods on the nutritional composition of food and human health.
[17, PDF page 2] In the first part of this article therefore, we critically review the evidence that organic farming methods improve the nutritional quality of food crops.
[18, PDF page 2] Moreover, we summarize our current understanding of how quality gains are linked to the implementation of the “innovations” introduced into conventional crop production during the intensification or “green revolution” of agriculture over the last 100 years.
[19, PDF page 2] In the second part of the article, we critically review the evidence for the range of health benefits related to organic food consumption.
[20, PDF page 2] Specifically, we describe and discuss the results from: (i) dietary intervention studies which have found that organic food consumption substantially reduces pesticide exposure in humans and affects feed intake, growth, hormone balances and immune system responsiveness in animal models; (ii) human cohort/epidemiological studies which have reported significant positive associations between organic food consumption and the lower incidence of a range of diseases including obesity, metabolic syndrome, cancer, hypospadias, pre-eclampsia, eczema and middle ear infections in infants; (iii) interactions and trade-offs between diet (e.g., whole-grain, fruit and vegetables and reduced red-meat consumption) and food types (organic versus conventional) concerning public health and future food security.
[21, PDF page 2] The article also identifies knowledge gaps and highlights the need for (i) longterm, factorial field experiments to understand the relative effects of agronomic and pedoclimatic drivers on crop quality and safety, and (ii) clinical trials and additional human cohort studies to confirm the positive health outcomes linked to organic food consumption.
[22, PDF page 2] The main conclusions from our review are that there is growing evidence that (i) agricultural intensification has resulted in a reduction in the nutritional quality of food and the sustainability of food production, and (ii) organic farming practices not only improve food quality and human health, but also food security.
[23, PDF page 2] This is particularly true where current nutritional guidelines (increasing whole-grain, fruit and vegetable products, while reducing red-meat consumption) are implemented.

claim.source_section_context:
[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 3.2. Evidence from Human Dietary Intervention and Cohort Studies
[66, PDF page 27] Several dietary intervention studies with humans and some human cohort studies have assessed the effect of organic versus conventional food consumption on urinary excretion of pesticide residues, but there is limited data on urinary excretion of other health relevant compounds (e.g., phenolics, other phytochemicals, antioxidants and mineral micronutrients).
[67, PDF page 27] These studies have consistently shown that organic food consumption results in significantly lower exposure to a range of pesticides, but identified no or only very small effects on the urinary excretion of other health relevant compounds [141,168,169,185–190]; this evidence has been described and discussed in detail in a recent systematic review by Vigar et al. [169].
[68, PDF page 27] The most controlled (during the 2-week intervention period participants consumed either only certified organic or only conventional foods) and comprehensive (in terms of the range of pesticides monitored) dietary intervention study estimated that changing to organic food consumption can reduce total pesticide exposure by more than 90% [ 141].
[69, PDF page 27] Interestingly, the same study also found that switching from habitual Western diets (with high meat and low fruit and vegetable consumption) to a healthy, traditional Mediterranean diet with low meat, and high fruit and vegetable consumption, resulted in 3–4 times higher insecticide and organophosphate exposure [ 141].
[70, PDF page 27] These results suggest that the effects of changing to organic food consumption, considering dietary pesticide intake and the associated potential negative health impacts, may be greater with a healthy diet.
[71, PDF page 27] The finding that organic food consumption can significantly reduce pesticide exposure is thought to be of relevance for human health, because there is increasing scientific evidence for the negative impacts of chronic dietary pesticide exposure, especially compounds that are suspected or proven to be neurotoxic and/or endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) [ 129–136].
[72, PDF page 27] Negative health effects of occupational and environmental exposure to pesticides are also well documented and predicted to increase in the future [129,130,132–136,191].
[73, PDF page 27] For example, a recent market analysis for pharmaceutical products that are used to treat acute carbamate and organophosphate poisoning in farmers and contractors that handle pesticides have predicted a significant increase in demand, especially in developing and underdeveloped countries, due to a predicted increase in pesticide use in these countries [191].
[74, PDF page 27] It should be pointed out that the European Commission and other government regulators set maximum residue limits (MRLs) for pesticides in food crops that are orders of magnitude below the concentrations that result in measurable toxicity symptoms in animal studies [128,161].
[75, PDF page 27] Regulators therefore consider pesticide residues below the MRLs as safe for consumers [128,129,161,192–194].
[76, PDF page 27] However, regulatory residue monitoring in Europe continues to find that a significant proportion of crop samples contain pesticide residues above the MRL [ 128], and there is increasing concern about the efficacy of the current regulatory pesticide approval system and the “safety” of pesticide residues below MRLs set by regulators [134–136].
[77, PDF page 27] One of the main concerns is that the current regulatory toxicological safety testing is based on Paracelsus’ 15th century assumption that “toxic effects” are greater at higher rather than lower doses (“the dose makes the poison”).
[78, PDF page 27] Pesticide safety testing is therefore usually based on one-generation animal studies (usually rodents) that assess the effect of high and moderate doses of chemicals.
[79, PDF page 27] Specifically, these tests determine the frequency and severity of death, disease symptoms, fetus malformations and/or low birth weights.
[80, PDF page 27] Results are then linearly extrapolated downwards and MRLs set at doses that are assumed to be safe [129,132,193–195].
[81, PDF page 27] However, many of the most widely used pesticides are suspected or confirmed endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs), which, like hormones, have (i) activity at very low doses and (ii) U-shaped and/or inverted U-shaped, non-monotonic dose-response curves [132–134,195–197].
[82, PDF page 27] This makes it impossible to predict negative health impacts associated with low-level dietary exposure based on the current regulatory, animal model-based toxicity tests.
[83, PDF page 27] Moreover, ECDs are increasingly recognized to lead to epigenetic alterations
[84, PDF page 28] and programming, which may eventually lead to an increased incidence in a variety of diseases (including obesity, type-2 diabetes, immune abnormalities and cancer) later in life, or in subsequent generations [132,195–198].
[85, PDF page 28] Epigenetic effects of ECDs can therefore only be accurately identified via extensive, multigenerational animal studies, but such tests are not usually required as part of standard regulatory pesticide safety evaluation protocols [195–198].
[86, PDF page 28] As a result, there is an urgent need to address these deficiencies, given the “health” and “societal” costs that may result from chronic exposure to EDCs both in Europe and globally [199,200].
[87, PDF page 28] There is also concern about the relatively high MRLs set by the EU for some widely used pesticides.
[88, PDF page 28] For example, MRLs for chlormequat (7 mg kg−1) and glyphosate (10 mg kg−1) are more than 10 times higher than those set for most other pesticides (0.01–0.4 mg kg−1) licensed for use in Europe [ 141,161,201,202].
[89, PDF page 28] In this context, it is important to consider that both pesticides are suspected endocrine-disrupting chemicals [203] and glyphosate was recently classified as a probable carcinogen [204].
[90, PDF page 28] Another limitation of the current regulatory toxicological evaluations is that they only require testing of individual active compounds, whereas testing of formulated products and combinations of pesticides is not usually required [129,132,193–195].
[91, PDF page 28] Moreover, the reliance of regulators on industry-commissioned (rather than independent) toxicological evaluations has recently been criticized [205,206].
[92, PDF page 28] A recent systematic review reported that there have been no controlled dietary intervention studies/clinical trials in which the effects of organic versus conventional food production on health outcomes has been studied [169].
[93, PDF page 28] However, there is increasing evidence from human cohort/epidemiological studies that organic food consumption is associated with significantly lower risks of a range of diseases including overweight/obesity [207], metabolic syndrome [208], certain cancers [209,210], hypospadias [211,212] pre-eclampsia [213], eczema [214] and middle ear infections (otitis media) [215].
[94, PDF page 28] This evidence has been discussed in detail in a recent systematic review by Vigar et al. [169].
[95, PDF page 28] Associations between disease incidence and pesticide exposure were only assessed in one of these observational studies, which found that the presence of metabolites of triazine herbicides in urine was positively associated with recurrent middle ear infections in infants [169,215].
[96, PDF page 28] It is important to note that there are now two European studies from France and the UK, which have reported that organic food consumption results in a lower incidence of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) [ 209,210] and that observational evidence for positive associations between NHL and exposure to organophosphates were the main reasons why glyphosate and other organophosphates are now as classified as probable carcinogens [204].
[97, PDF page 28] Lower pesticide exposure from fruit and vegetable consumption was recently found to be associated with improved reproductive health parameters in both men and women[216,217].
[98, PDF page 28] Similarly , a reduced incidence of breast cancer among postmenopausal women in the NutriNet- Santé cohort was linked to (i) low dietary exposure to synthetic pesticides such as chlorpyriphos, imazalil, malathion and thiabendazole [218], and (ii) high organic food consumption [210].

[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] Abstract.
[18] Moreover, we summarize our current understanding of how quality gains are linked to the implementation of the “innovations” introduced into conventional crop production during the intensification or “green revolution” of agriculture over the last 100 years.
[19] In the second part of the article, we critically review the evidence for the range of health benefits related to organic food consumption.
[20] Specifically, we describe and discuss the results from: (i) dietary intervention studies which have found that organic food consumption substantially reduces pesticide exposure in humans and affects feed intake, growth, hormone balances and immune system responsiveness in animal models; (ii) human cohort/epidemiological studies which have reported significant positive associations between organic food consumption and the lower incidence of a range of diseases including obesity, metabolic syndrome, cancer, hypospadias, pre-eclampsia, eczema and middle ear infections in infants; (iii) interactions and trade-offs between diet (e.g., whole-grain, fruit and vegetables and reduced red-meat consumption) and food types (organic versus conventional) concerning public health and future food security.
[21] The article also identifies knowledge gaps and highlights the need for (i) longterm, factorial field experiments to understand the relative effects of agronomic and pedoclimatic drivers on crop quality and safety, and (ii) clinical trials and additional human cohort studies to confirm the positive health outcomes linked to organic food consumption.
[22] The main conclusions from our review are that there is growing evidence that (i) agricultural intensification has resulted in a reduction in the nutritional quality of food and the sustainability of food production, and (ii) organic farming practices not only improve food quality and human health, but also food security.
